In laboratory cultures of Alaskozetes antarcticus maintained at a constant temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C], egg development proceeds slowly, with the first active protonymphs emerging approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days] after oviposition. The larval stage remains dependent on these reserves until the trophic switch to active feeding is fully established, after which growth proceeds in earnest. Newly hatched mites begin to forage on microbial biofilms, with feeding activity accelerating as they transition through the protonymphal and deutonymphal instars under the cold conditions typical of their maritime Antarctic habitat.

The transition from the larval stage through metamorphosis represents a critical developmental bottleneck for Alaskozetes antarcticus. At the point of metamorphic climax, when the hexapod larva reorganizes its body plan and enters the tritonymphal instar, the dry weight recorded is 3.6 micrograms . This value, though modest, signifies the successful accumulation of resources necessary for this morphological transformation. Comparative data from related oribatid species suggest that the efficiency of this allometric shift is tightly linked to local food quality and the duration of the growing season. Post-metamorphic juveniles continue to feed actively, gradually increasing in mass as they progress toward the sub-adult stage. The dry weight at the onset of puberty, marking the initiation of gametogenesis, reaches approximately 52 micrograms  when measured in individuals reared under optimal conditions. This pubertal threshold represents the culmination of months of sustained foraging and nutrient assimilation during the juvenile period.

Individuals that attain reproductive maturity exhibit a notably extended lifespan for an arthropod of such diminutive size, with maximum longevity recorded at 2190 days [am = 2190 days] in captive populations maintained at 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This duration is unusually protracted relative to most temperate oribatid mites and aligns with the slow life-history pace characteristic of Antarctic ectotherms. The time elapsed from hatching to the attainment of sexual maturity under a constant thermal regime of 0 °C [T = 0 °C] is 1825 days from hatching [tp = 1825 days from hatching], or roughly five years, a remarkably extended developmental period that reflects the constraints imposed by low temperatures on cellular metabolism and growth rates. Following puberty, adults enter a reproductively viable phase that lasts for several additional years before the onset of reproductive senescence. The eventual physiological death of these individuals typically occurs through progressive organ failure rather than predation, given the scarcity of natural enemies in their extreme habitat.

Reproductive output in Alaskozetes antarcticus is characterized by low fecundity per event but sustained breeding effort over the long adult lifespan. Egg clutches are typically small, with females producing between 4 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 4 and 6 eggs per clutch], though exceptional clutches of up to 14 eggs [N_R_i = clutches of up to 14 eggs] have been observed in captive individuals under high-quality dietary regimes at 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. The frequency of reproductive events is also modest, with females producing approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year] under these same thermal conditions, yielding a maximum reproductive rate equivalent to roughly 5 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 5 eggs per year]. This conservative reproductive strategy contrasts sharply with that of smaller, faster-growing temperate oribatids, and likely represents an adaptation to the extreme seasonality and limited resource availability of Antarctic fellfield ecosystems. The energetic investment per egg is substantial, given the need to provision each offspring with sufficient yolk for prolonged embryonic development.

The ultimate body size attained by adult Alaskozetes antarcticus reflects the cumulative growth achieved over their extended developmental period. Maximum dry weight recorded in fully mature, reproductively active adults reaches 80 micrograms , while the corresponding ultimate wet weight, measured immediately after molt before desiccation losses occur, is 180 micrograms [Wwi = 180 micrograms]. This wet-to-dry mass ratio of approximately 2.25 is consistent with values reported for other aquatic and semi-terrestrial microarthropods inhabiting cold environments, where body water content is often elevated to prevent freezing injury. The adult body mass, though still microscopic by vertebrate standards, represents a more than forty-fold increase from the 2-microgram dry weight at birth (2 micrograms)  noted earlier. Such substantial growth over the course of the five-year pre-reproductive period underscores the slow but steady accumulation of somatic tissue characteristic of this species. Field-collected specimens from Signy Island generally fall within this size range, though individuals from more exposed, nutrient-poor sites occasionally fail to reach the maximal values reported here, indicating that local resource gradients impose constraints on the ultimate size attainable.
